title: Body Systems and Plant Root and Shoot Systems
summary: Learners describe how the muscular, skeletal, digestive, circulatory, and respiratory systems work. They observe plant roots and shoots and explain why each part is important. They make labeled diagrams and begin a poster that classifies a Philippine plant or animal by habitat.

competencies.text: Describe in simple terms how the following human body systems work: muscular, skeletal, digestive, circulatory, and respiratory.
Observe the root and shoot system in plants and describe why they are important.

timing.basis: Science is taught five times a week, 45 minutes a session, in Grades 3–10: DepEd Order No. 010, s. 2024 (Tables 3, 5 and 6) and DepEd Order No. 012, s. 2024 (§2.a, which also allows uniform 50, 55 or 60-minute periods). Applied to the SY 2026–2027 three-term calendar.

guide.bigIdea: The human body has organ systems that work together to keep us alive, and plants have root and shoot systems that keep them alive.
guide.whyItMatters: Understanding body systems helps learners make everyday choices that keep their bodies healthy. Knowing how plant roots and shoots work helps them care for rice, vegetables, and other plants at home and in the community—especially during heavy rains, when roots stop soil from washing away.

background.heading: The human body: a team of systems
paragraphs: The human body is organized like a team. Cells of the same type group into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems. For this week's competency, learners only need to describe five systems in simple terms: muscular, skeletal, digestive, circulatory, and respiratory. They should understand each system's main job and how the systems work together. For example, digested food nutrients enter the blood through the circulatory system, and oxygen from the respiratory system is carried by the same blood to every cell.

Textbook diagrams often show these systems separately, but they are always working at the same time. A useful image is that the digestive and respiratory systems bring in supplies, the circulatory system delivers them, and the muscular and skeletal systems use them to move.

background.heading: Muscular and skeletal systems: movement and protection
paragraphs: The skeletal system includes bones, cartilage, and the joints where bones meet. Bones are living tissue. They give the body shape, support its weight, and protect soft organs: the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs, and the backbone protects the spinal cord. Bones also serve as levers. A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a point; in the body, bones are the bars and joints are the turning points.

The muscular system has three kinds of muscle: skeletal muscle attached to bones, smooth muscle in organs such as the stomach and blood vessels, and cardiac muscle in the heart. Skeletal muscles are voluntary because we decide to move them; smooth and cardiac muscle work without us thinking. Muscles can only pull or shorten, never push. To bend and straighten an elbow, the biceps muscle on the front of the upper arm contracts and shortens while the triceps on the back relaxes; to straighten, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. This is why muscles often work in pairs.

background.heading: Digestive system: breaking down food
paragraphs: The digestive system is a long tube with organs that work together to break food into small enough pieces for the body to absorb. Mechanical digestion is physical breaking—chewing in the mouth and churning in the stomach. Chemical digestion begins in the mouth (saliva starts breaking down starch), continues in the stomach (acid and enzymes start breaking down protein), and is completed mainly in the small intestine, where juices from the pancreas and liver finish the job.

The path is: mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. Most chemical digestion happens in the mouth and small intestine; the stomach mainly churns and mixes food with acid and enzymes to break down proteins. The small intestine is where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood through its folded, finger-like lining. The large intestine absorbs water and salts and turns the remaining undigested material into stool. A common simplification says 'the stomach digests food'; it is more accurate that digestion starts in the mouth and finishes mainly in the small intestine.

background.heading: Circulatory and respiratory systems: transport and gas exchange
paragraphs: The circulatory system is the body's transport network. The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers. It pushes blood through blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry blood back, and capillaries are tiny vessels where materials pass between blood and cells. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, and hormones to cells and removes carbon dioxide and other wastes.

The respiratory system brings air into the body. Air enters through the nose or mouth, passes through the trachea (windpipe), and reaches the lungs. In the lungs, air moves into tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen moves from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air. The diaphragm, a sheet of muscle below the lungs, helps pull air in and push it out. The brain monitors carbon dioxide levels and controls how fast and deep we breathe.
The two systems meet in the lungs: the respiratory system loads oxygen into the blood and removes carbon dioxide, and the circulatory system carries those gases between the lungs and all body cells.

background.heading: Plant root system: anchoring and absorbing
paragraphs: A plant's root system usually grows below ground. Its two big jobs are to anchor the plant in place and to absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil. Root hairs—tiny extensions on young roots—greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Roots also store food in some plants, such as sweet potato and radish, but that is a secondary role.

The root tip is protected by a root cap and grows downward. Many Philippine grasses and crops, like rice and cogon, have fibrous root systems that spread widely and hold soil tightly, which helps reduce erosion on sloping land. Mangroves have specialized roots that hold them in soft coastal mud.

background.heading: Plant shoot system: supporting and food-making
paragraphs: The shoot system is the above-ground part of the plant: stems, leaves, buds, flowers, and fruits. The stem holds leaves and flowers up to the light and contains vascular bundles—strands of xylem and phloem. Xylem transports water and minerals from the roots upward; phloem transports sugars made in the leaves to other parts of the plant. The leaf is the main food-making organ. In photosynthesis, leaves use light energy, carbon dioxide from the air, and water to make sugar and release oxygen.

Leaves also lose water vapor through small pores, a process called transpiration. This water loss pulls water up from the roots, like drinking through a straw. In Philippine vegetables like kangkong, the stems and leaves we eat are part of the shoot system and carry out photosynthesis and transpiration.

misconceptions.belief: Bones are dry, white, and dead.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: They see clean, dry skeletons in pictures or museums.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Bones are living tissue. They have blood vessels and nerves, can grow, and can heal after a break.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Bones are living: they grow as you grow, they hurt when broken (they have nerves), and they heal after a break — a dead thing cannot grow or heal. Blood vessels run inside bones, but the warmth you feel at your wrist is from blood in your skin, not from the bone.

misconceptions.belief: Muscles push bones to move them.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: Everyday pushing movements feel like the muscle is pushing.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Muscles can only pull or shorten, never push. Pairs of muscles pull bones in opposite directions.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Use a rubber band tied to two cardboard strips. Show that a rubber band can only pull, never push. Then connect the rubber band to the biceps pulling the arm.

misconceptions.belief: The stomach is where all digestion happens.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: Many diagrams focus on the stomach, and learners feel food 'drop' into the belly.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Digestion starts in the mouth with chewing and saliva. Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Trace the food path on a large body outline and place a star at the small intestine as the 'absorption station'. Emphasize that the stomach mostly churns and starts breaking down proteins.

misconceptions.belief: Plants get their food from the soil.
misconceptions.whyLearnersThinkIt: Roots are in the soil, and learners see fertilizer added to plants and think it is plant food.
misconceptions.correctIdea: Plants make their own food through photosynthesis in the leaves. Roots absorb water and minerals, not sugar.
misconceptions.howToAddress: Show a mung bean sprout growing in cotton with only water. Ask where its food comes from. Explain: 'First the sprout uses the food packed inside the seed (the thick seed halves). Once green leaves open, the plant makes its own sugar from sunlight, water and air. The cotton and water supply only water — no food.'

studentQuestions.question: Why do muscles always work in pairs?
studentQuestions.answer: A muscle can only shorten and pull. It cannot lengthen itself to push. To move a bone back and forth, you need one muscle on each side. When one contracts, the other relaxes.

studentQuestions.question: If plants make food in their leaves, why do we add fertilizer or compost to the soil?
studentQuestions.answer: The food a plant makes is sugar, but plants also need minerals like nitrogen and phosphorus from the soil to build proteins and other important parts. Fertilizer and compost supply those minerals, not the plant's main food.

studentQuestions.question: Why can't we hold our breath forever?
studentQuestions.answer: The brain senses rising carbon dioxide in the blood. When carbon dioxide builds up, the brain sends signals to the diaphragm to contract, so you are forced to breathe. Holding your breath increases carbon dioxide and creates a strong urge to breathe.

studentQuestions.question: Do bones have blood inside them?
studentQuestions.answer: Yes, bones are living tissue. They contain blood vessels and nerves. That is why a broken bone hurts and can heal over time.

studentQuestions.question: Why are some roots thick, like sweet potato?
studentQuestions.answer: Some roots store extra food made by the leaves. The plant uses this stored food to survive dry times or to grow new parts. A sweet potato is a storage root.

studentQuestions.question: How does water get all the way to the top of a tall coconut tree?
studentQuestions.answer: Leaves release water vapor through tiny pores. This loss of water pulls more water up through tiny tubes called xylem, like drinking from a straw. Roots also absorb water, and this pull helps it travel upward.

localExamples.example: A carabao pulling a plow in a rice field.
localExamples.connection: The carabao's skeletal muscles pull on its bones at the joints to move its legs, and its skeleton supports its heavy body.

localExamples.example: Rice plants growing in a flooded paddy.
localExamples.connection: Rice roots absorb water and minerals and hold the plant in soft mud. The shoot system—stem and leaves—makes food.

localExamples.example: Kangkong stems and leaves sold in a wet market.
localExamples.connection: The part sold is the shoot system. Its stems hold leaves up and transport water, while leaves photosynthesize.

localExamples.example: Cogon grass on a roadside slope.
localExamples.connection: Cogon spreads by creeping underground stems (rhizomes) with many fibrous roots. Together they form a dense mat that holds soil and reduces washing away during heavy rain.
