days.title: Muscles and Bones: How We Move
days.objective: Learners will be able to describe how muscles pull on bones at joints to produce movement and how bones protect soft organs.
materials: 1 cardboard strip (about 30 cm × 5 cm) per teacher demonstration
2 rubber bands per teacher demonstration
1 sheet of manila paper or bond paper per pair for drawing
Crayons or pencils for labeling (1 set per pair)
1 stopwatch or phone timer for the teacher
Optional: 1 pre-germinated mung bean in a clear cup for the extension

flow.teacher: Stand at the front and bend your arm slowly. Ask: 'What moves when I bend my arm?' [The arm; the elbow; the muscles; the bones.] Write 'move' on the board. Then ask: 'Put your hand on your upper arm and bend your elbow. What do you feel?' [Something gets hard; a muscle.] Let 2–3 learners answer. Tell them: 'Today we will find out how muscles and bones work together so we can move.' Do not confirm answers yet — just collect ideas.
flow.learners: Learners watch the teacher, then feel their own upper arm while bending the elbow. They raise hands to share what they feel. In a large class, ask learners to tell a partner first, then call on 2–3 pairs.

flow.teacher: Read the objective aloud in simple words: 'Today we will learn how muscles pull on bones at joints to make us move, and how bones protect soft organs.' Ask: 'Why is it important to know this?' [So we know how our body moves; so we can take care of our bones and muscles.] Show the next slide and point to the three key words: bones, muscles, joints. Tell learners that by the end of the lesson they will answer one question on paper.
flow.learners: Learners listen and repeat the three key words. They think of one reason why learning about bones and muscles is useful and share with a partner.

flow.teacher: Show the slide about bones. Explain: 'Your skeleton is all the bones in your body. It gives your body shape and holds you up.' Ask: 'What would happen if we had no bones?' [We would be floppy; we could not stand.] Then show the slide about bones protecting organs. Point to your head, chest, and back. Ask: 'Which bone protects the brain?' [The skull.] 'Which bones protect the heart and lungs?' [The rib cage.] Let learners gently touch their own ribs and skull. Correct the idea that bones are dead: 'Bones are living. They have blood vessels and nerves, they grow, and they can heal when broken.'
flow.learners: Learners touch their own skull and ribs gently. They answer the teacher's questions and listen to the correction about bones being living tissue.

flow.teacher: Show the slide about muscles. Explain: 'Muscles can only pull or shorten. They cannot push.' Demonstrate with TWO rigid strips joined at one end with a paper fastener or tape hinge, with a rubber band on each side across the joint. Script: 'The two strips are two bones; the fastener is the elbow joint. The bones stay stiff — the rubber band pulls one bone around the joint.' Pull one rubber band to bend the hinge, then release and pull the other to straighten it. Ask: 'Can the rubber band push the strip back?' [No, it can only pull.] Then show the muscle pairs slide: 'When the biceps pulls, the arm bends. When the triceps pulls, the arm straightens. They work as a pair.' Ask: 'Which muscle pulls when I bend my arm?' [The biceps.] 'Which one pulls when I straighten it?' [The triceps.] Correct the wrong idea that muscles push bones.
flow.learners: Learners watch the demonstration. In pairs, they feel their own biceps and triceps while bending and straightening the arm. They answer the teacher's questions.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide. Say: 'In pairs, one partner slowly bends and straightens the arm. The other gently presses the upper arm to feel the biceps and triceps. Then draw the arm and label the bones, biceps, triceps, and elbow joint.' Give 8 minutes. Walk around and ask: 'Which muscle is hard when the arm bends?' [The biceps.] 'What do we call the place where two bones meet?' [A joint.] Remind learners to press gently and never twist a partner's arm. In a large class, assign one partner to draw and the other to label, then swap. After 8 minutes, show the joint slide and explain: 'A joint is where two bones meet and allow movement. Your elbow is a hinge joint — it bends like a door.' Ask: 'Where else do you have joints?' [Knee, shoulder, hip, wrist.]
flow.learners: In pairs, learners take turns bending and straightening the arm while the partner gently feels the upper arm. They draw the arm on manila paper and label the bones, biceps, triceps, and elbow joint. They answer questions about joints.

flow.teacher: Show the summary slide. Ask learners to help complete the sentences: 'The skeletal system gives my body ___ and ___.' [Shape; support.] 'Bones protect ___ organs.' [Soft.] 'Muscles can only ___, not push.' [Pull.] 'A ___ is where two bones meet.' [Joint.] Write the summary on the board and ask learners to copy it. Remind them: 'The muscular system and skeletal system work as a team.'
flow.learners: Learners answer the fill-in-the-blank questions aloud. They copy the summary sentences into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide and read the question aloud. Give 1 minute for learners to choose an answer on paper. Do not reveal the answer yet. Then show the reveal slide and explain why. Finally, give a different exit ticket on a small slip of paper: 'Draw an arm bending. Label the bone, the joint, and the muscle that pulls. Write one sentence: why can a muscle not push the bone back?' Collect the slips. If many learners choose A, re-show the muscle pairs slide and repeat the rubber band demonstration.
flow.learners: Learners answer the check question on paper. They watch the reveal and check their answer. Then they answer the exit-ticket question on a slip of paper and submit it.

expectedObservations: When the arm bends, the biceps on top of the upper arm feels firm or hard.
When the arm straightens, the triceps at the back of the upper arm feels firm.
Learners can point to the elbow and say it is a joint where two bones meet.
Learners can name the skull as the bone that protects the brain and the ribs as bones that protect the heart and lungs.
In drawings, learners label the biceps and triceps on opposite sides of the upper arm bone.

check.question: Which statement is correct about muscles and bones?
check.answer: Muscles pull on bones to move them; muscles cannot push.
check.why: Muscles can only shorten and pull. To move a bone back and forth, a pair of muscles pulls in opposite directions.

days.support: For learners who struggle, give them a labeled diagram with the words biceps, triceps, bone, and joint already written, and ask them to draw arrows showing which way each muscle pulls. Let them feel their own arm again while you say the names slowly. Pair them with a learner who can model the arm bend. Accept oral answers instead of written labels if writing is a barrier.
days.extension: Ask fast finishers to use the two-strip hinge model (two rigid strips joined by a paper fastener) to show how the elbow bends. They write one sentence: 'My elbow is a hinge joint because the two bones move around a fixed point like a door hinge.' They can also list three joints in the body and the movement each allows (knee bends, shoulder circles, hip rotates).
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add a 5-minute gallery walk where pairs post their labeled arm drawings and give one star and one question to another pair. Add a 3-minute teacher-led discussion of the question 'What would happen if muscles and bones did not work together?' [We could not move; bones would have no pulling force.] Use the extra time for the extension hinge-joint task with the whole class.

days.title: The Digestive System: Food's Journey
days.objective: Learners will be able to trace the path of food through the digestive organs and describe what happens at each main stop.
materials: 1 zip-top plastic bag per demonstration (teacher's bag; 1 backup)
1 slice of bread (or a small piece of pandesal) for the demonstration
About 120 mL of water in a small bottle or jug for the demonstration
1 large sheet of manila paper or cartolina per pair (about 30 sheets for a class of 60)
Crayons or colored pencils: red, blue, green, brown (enough sets for pairs to share)
1 printed body outline per pair, OR 1 large body outline drawn on the board for learners to copy
Masking tape for posting pair work
1 clean cloth or paper towel for wiping the bag and table

flow.teacher: Start with the question slide. Ask: 'What happens to your food after you swallow it?' Let 3–4 learners answer. Accept all answers without correcting yet; write 2-3 of them on the board so you can return to them later. Expected answers: 'It goes to the stomach', 'It becomes poop', 'It goes down'. Then show the vocabulary slide and read each term aloud; have the class repeat 'digestion' and 'esophagus' twice. Say: 'Today we follow one bite of food from the mouth to the end.' Keep this quick — 5 minutes only.
flow.learners: Learners answer the question aloud, listen to classmates, and repeat the new words. In a large class, call on learners from different rows so more voices are heard.

flow.teacher: Show the purpose slide. Read the goal together: 'We can trace the path of food and say what happens at each stop.' Tell learners they will draw this path on a big body outline in pairs, and that at the end they will answer one question on paper. Point to the food-path drawing and say: 'This is the journey we will learn today.' Do not give the order of organs yet — learners will build it.
flow.learners: Learners read the goal with the teacher and look at the drawing. They keep their seats; no materials are given out yet.

flow.teacher: Show the mouth slide. Ask: 'Why do we chew food?' [To break it into smaller pieces; it mixes with saliva.] Explain that digestion starts in the mouth: teeth grind food and saliva makes it wet and starts breaking it down. Then show the esophagus and stomach slide. Ask: 'Does food fall down your throat by gravity?' [No — the esophagus squeezes it down in waves.] Then, at the demonstration table, put the bread slice in the zip-top bag, add a little water, seal the bag well, and squeeze gently. Say: 'The stomach is a bag of muscle. It squeezes and mixes food with juices.' Safety: seal the bag fully and squeeze gently so it does not burst; do not taste the mixture; wash hands after handling bread and the bag; wipe the table afterwards. Do not let learners open the bag. If a learner asks about stomach acid, say the stomach has juices that help break down food, without naming chemicals.
flow.learners: Learners watch the demonstration from their seats. Ask them to describe what they see happening to the bread [it gets soft, mushy, breaks apart]. Pairs whisper one observation to each other, then 2 learners share with the class.

flow.teacher: Show the small and large intestine slide. Explain: most nutrients are taken into the body in the small intestine, and the large intestine takes in water and forms waste. Then show the activity slide and give instructions: 'In pairs, draw a body outline and draw arrows showing the path: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Label each part and write one short job beside it. You have 10 minutes.' Hand out manila paper and crayons. For a large class, assign one pair per table to get materials, or have materials pre-set on tables before class. Walk around and ask: 'Which organ takes in most nutrients?' [small intestine] 'Which one takes in water?' [large intestine] Common wrong answer: learners draw the stomach as the biggest stop or say all digestion happens there. Respond: 'The stomach starts the job; the small intestine finishes it.' Circulate and check labels. Give a 2-minute warning before time is up.
flow.learners: Pairs draw and label the food path on manila paper using colored arrows, then write one short job for each organ. At the end, pairs exchange papers with a nearby pair to check that all five stops are labeled.

flow.teacher: Show the check question slide and read it aloud. Give 30 seconds of quiet thinking time, then have learners raise hands to choose an option. Do not say if it is right yet. Count hands for each option. Then show the reveal slide and explain: most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine; the stomach mostly churns food and starts breaking down proteins, and digestion also begins in the mouth. Blood is always red — brighter red when it carries more oxygen, darker red when it carries less. Blue is only a drawing colour we use to show blood heading back to the lungs. Return to the board answers from the start of the lesson and ask: 'Which answers do we keep? Which do we change?' [e.g., 'It goes to the stomach' is only the first stop, not the whole journey.]
flow.learners: Learners think quietly, then vote by raising hands. After the reveal, they compare their partner's drawing with the correct answer and fix any wrong labels with a crayon.

flow.teacher: Exit ticket: give each learner a small slip of paper (or have them use the back of their notebook). Read the question aloud and write it on the board. Say: 'Answer in one sentence. No talking, no copying.' Question: 'A learner eats a banana. Trace two stops the banana makes and say one job of each stop.' Expected answer: 'It starts in the mouth, where teeth and saliva break it down; then it goes down the esophagus to the stomach, where it is churned with juices' — or any two correct stops with correct jobs, such as small intestine absorbing nutrients or large intestine taking in water and forming waste. Collect the slips. While collecting, tell learners the goal of their poster from the week continues tomorrow: keep their drawings for the gallery walk. If time remains, ask 2 learners to share their two stops aloud.
flow.learners: Each learner writes a one-sentence answer on a slip of paper or notebook and passes it forward. Learners who finish early draw one organ from today's journey and write its job underneath.

expectedObservations: The bread in the bag becomes soft and mushy when squeezed with water, showing how the stomach churns and mixes food with juices.
Learners can name five stops in order: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.
Learners notice that digestion starts in the mouth, not the stomach.
Learners label the small intestine as the place where most nutrients are absorbed.
Learners show the esophagus as a tube that squeezes food down to the stomach, not one that lets food fall.

check.question: A learner eats a banana. Trace two stops the banana makes and say one job of each stop.
check.answer: Any two correct stops with a correct job, e.g. 'In the mouth, teeth and saliva break the banana into smaller pieces; then it goes down the esophagus to the stomach, where it is churned with juices.'
check.why: Digestion begins in the mouth with chewing and saliva; the esophagus squeezes food down; the stomach churns food with juices; the small intestine absorbs most nutrients; the large intestine absorbs water and forms waste. Any two stops correctly matched to their job shows the learner can trace and explain the journey.

days.support: For learners who struggle, give a word bank of the five stops on the board and let them copy the words before drawing. Pair them with a stronger partner and ask them to point to each organ on the body outline before drawing the arrow. Accept a drawing with two or three labeled stops as partial progress, then help them add the rest. Read the exit-ticket question aloud twice and let them answer orally to you first, then write.
days.extension: Ask fast finishers to add a 'what happens if' box to their drawing: 'What happens if a learner does not chew food well?' [bigger pieces reach the stomach, which must work harder to churn them; they can help by answering that chewing helps digestion start right.] They can also add the liver and pancreas as helpers that send juices to the small intestine to help digestion, without naming chemicals.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add 5–10 minutes after the gallery of drawings: pairs stand and present their food-path drawing to another pair in 30 seconds each. Add a quick sorting game on the board: write the five stops on the board and have learners match job cards (breaks food with teeth and saliva; squeezes food down; churns food with juices; absorbs most nutrients; absorbs water and forms waste) to the correct stop. Use the remaining minutes for the exit ticket so every learner finishes.

days.title: Circulation and Breathing: Delivery and Air
days.objective: Learners will be able to describe how the heart pumps blood to carry oxygen and nutrients and how the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
materials: stopwatch or phone timer (1 per teacher)
chalkboard and red and blue chalk (or whiteboard and red and blue markers)
learner notebooks and pencils (1 each)
large body outline on manila paper (1 per group of 4–6) — optional for the loop diagram
clear floor space for gentle jumps

flow.teacher: Begin with the Day 3 title slide. Say: 'Last time we followed food through the body. Today we look at how the body delivers oxygen and food to every cell, and how it removes waste gas.' Ask: 'When you run fast, what changes in your body?' Expect answers: faster breathing, faster heartbeat, sweating, tired legs. Accept all; write 'breathe faster' and 'heart beats faster' on the board. Ask: 'Why do you think your heart beats faster?' Take 2–3 guesses without judging. Say: 'Today we will find out.'
flow.learners: Listen, think, and share answers with the class. In large classes, ask learners to turn to a partner first, then call on 2–3 pairs.

flow.teacher: Show the lesson purpose slide. Read the objective aloud: 'Today we will describe how the heart pumps blood to carry oxygen and nutrients, and how the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.' Say: 'By the end, you should be able to explain why your breathing speeds up after jumping.' Ask one learner to repeat the objective in their own words. Tell learners they will count their own pulse and do gentle jumps later, so they need clear floor space.
flow.learners: Listen and restate the goal in their own words. Clear bags and chairs to make safe space for jumping.

flow.teacher: Show the concept slide on the heart. Say: 'The heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood through tubes called blood vessels. It works all the time.' Ask: 'Where can you feel your heart beating?' Expect: wrist, neck, chest. Show the vocabulary slide for pulse and blood vessels. Then show the concept slide on blood's job: 'Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries carbon dioxide away.' Say: 'Red chalk will show blood carrying oxygen; blue chalk will show blood carrying carbon dioxide.' Avoid saying breathing is respiration; say breathing brings oxygen into the blood.
flow.learners: Listen, point to places where they can feel their heartbeat, and copy the two vocabulary terms into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide. Model the pulse count: press two fingers (not the thumb) on the inside of the wrist below the thumb. Say: 'Count silently while I time 15 seconds.' Safety: Use wrist pulse only; never press on the neck. Press lightly. Run the seated count, then have learners stand and do 10 gentle jumps, then count again. Safety: clear floor space before jumping; learners with difficulty breathing or asthma may count a partner's pulse on the wrist or count breaths instead. Ask: 'What happened to your pulse after jumping?' Expect: it went up. Ask: 'Why?' Expect: muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. Record both numbers on the board. Then show the air path slide: 'Air goes in through your nose (or mouth) → down the windpipe (trachea) → into the lungs → oxygen passes into the blood.'
flow.learners: In pairs, count each other's pulse for 15 seconds while seated, do 10 gentle jumps, and count again. Record both numbers. Report answers to the class.

flow.teacher: Show the heart-lungs-body loop slide. Draw a simple loop on the board: lungs → heart → body → heart → lungs. Use red for oxygen-rich blood going to the body and blue for carbon dioxide-rich blood going back to the lungs. Say: 'The heart and lungs work as a team. The lungs add oxygen and remove carbon dioxide; the heart pumps the blood that carries them.' Ask learners to copy the loop into their notebooks and label oxygen in and carbon dioxide out.
flow.learners: Copy the loop diagram into notebooks and label the arrows: oxygen coming in, carbon dioxide going out.

flow.teacher: Show the check slide with the multiple-choice question. Read the question and choices aloud. Give 1 minute for learners to think, then have them show answers by raising fingers (1, 2, 3, or 4). Click to the reveal slide and discuss why the answer is correct. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'Why does your breathing speed up after jumping?' Collect papers. Note common wrong answers such as 'because the heart stops' or 'because lungs get tired' and address them next meeting.
flow.learners: Answer the check question by raising fingers, then write the exit-ticket answer on a small paper and submit.

expectedObservations: Pulse count is higher after 10 gentle jumps than when seated.
Learners can point to the wrist or neck to feel their pulse.
Learners explain that working muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide.
Learners can name the heart as a pump and the lungs as the place where oxygen enters the blood.

check.question: Why does your breathing speed up after jumping?
check.answer: To bring in more oxygen and remove the extra carbon dioxide made by working muscles.
check.why: Working muscles use more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. The brain senses the change and makes you breathe faster.

days.support: Learners who struggle to find a pulse can place a hand on the chest to feel the heartbeat, or count a partner's pulse. Pair them with a confident learner. For learners who cannot jump, allow them to count breaths or do gentle arm movements while seated. Use the loop diagram on the board as a reference during the exit ticket; remind them that the heart pumps and the lungs exchange gases.
days.extension: Ask learners to draw and label a simple heart-lungs-body loop in their notebooks, using red arrows for oxygen-rich blood and blue arrows for carbon dioxide-rich blood. Challenge them to write one sentence explaining why the heart and lungs must work together.
days.longerPeriod: Add a 10-minute group activity: groups of 4–6 draw a large body outline on manila paper and add the heart, lungs, and arrows showing oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. Groups explain their diagram to another group. Include a short discussion of what happens to breathing and pulse during rest versus exercise, using the recorded pulse numbers.

days.title: Plant Roots and Shoots: Below and Above
days.objective: Learners will be able to observe a germinating seed and describe the root and shoot systems and why each is important for the plant.
materials: Pre-germinated mung bean seeds in clear plastic cups with cotton, 1 cup per pair (about 20 cups for 40 learners)
Extra clear cups with cotton and dry mung bean seeds for comparison, 2–3
Clean water in a small bottle for misting cotton, 1 per group of 4–6
Hand lenses, 1 per pair (or share among 4 learners if limited)
Bond paper or science notebook pages, 1 per learner
Pencils, crayons or colored pencils (red and blue if available), enough to share
Manila paper and markers for group diagrams, 1 sheet per group of 4–6
Printed or drawn plant diagram (root system and shoot system) on manila paper or the board, 1 large copy
Pictures or actual samples of cogon grass and kangkong, 1 set per class (optional but helpful)
Masking tape for posting group work
Cloth or paper towels for spills, 2–3

flow.teacher: Start with a quick recall of the week: 'We learned how the body moves, digests food, and moves blood and air. Today we look at living things that do not have bones or a heart. What living things are these?' [Plants.] Show the day slide and the first question slide. Ask: 'Where do you think the roots of a plant grow? Why?' [Down into the soil; to get water and hold the plant.] Accept all answers without judging yet. Tell learners that today they will look closely at a real sprouting seed and find out what each part does.
flow.learners: Look at the screen and answer orally. In a large class, ask learners to first whisper their answer to a partner, then call on 3–4 pairs to share with the class.

flow.teacher: State the goal in learner-friendly words: 'Today we will observe a germinating mung bean seed, draw what we see, and describe why the root system and the shoot system are important.' Point to the two vocabulary words on the screen: root and shoot system. Say: 'By the end of the lesson, you should be able to point to the root system and the shoot system on a plant and tell one important job of each.' Show the vocabulary slide and read each term aloud; have the class repeat 'root system' and 'shoot system' once.
flow.learners: Listen, repeat the two key terms, and copy the two vocabulary meanings into their science notebooks.

flow.teacher: Show the concept slide 'Root Grow Down, Shoots Grow Up' and the picture of a germinating seed. Explain: 'When a seed sprouts, the root usually comes out first and grows down. The shoot grows up.' Ask: 'Why is it useful for the root to grow down?' [To reach water in the soil and to hold the plant steady.] Then show the concept slide about roots and ask: 'What do roots take from the soil?' [Water and minerals.] Correct the common idea that plants eat soil: roots take in water and minerals, but the plant makes its own food in the leaves. Before the activity, give the safety reminder: 'Wash your hands after handling the cups and cotton. Do not eat the seeds or anything in the cups. Do not open the cups or pull out the seedlings.'
flow.learners: Watch, answer the teacher's questions orally, and note the safety rules. They keep hands on their desks until the cups are given out.

flow.teacher: Show the activity slide. Give each pair one pre-germinated cup and one hand lens. Say: 'Look closely. Find the root and the shoot. Which one is longer? Which way does each grow?' Give 3 minutes to observe, then ask pairs to draw and label their seedling on paper: root, shoot, and leaves. Next, post the large plant diagram and ask groups of 4–6 to label the root system and shoot system and write one job for each part. Hand out manila paper and markers later, if using group posters. If a learner says 'the plant eats soil,' respond: 'Roots take in water and minerals, but the leaves make the food.' Circulate and ask: 'Why is it important for the stem to hold the leaves up?' [So leaves can get sunlight.] Classroom management: appoint one materials monitor per group to return cups and lenses; keep walkways clear and cups on the table, not the floor. Remind everyone to wash hands when the activity ends.
flow.learners: In pairs, observe the seedling with a hand lens, then draw and label the root, shoot, and leaves on paper. In groups of 4–6, label the plant diagram with root system and shoot system and write one job for each part. Wash hands after handling cups, cotton, and seeds.

flow.teacher: Bring the class back together. Show the check slide and ask each learner to choose an answer on their paper or show fingers: 1, 2, 3, or 4. Do not reveal yet. Then show the reveal slide and explain: 'The root system is usually below ground. It takes in water and minerals and holds the plant in place.' Ask a follow-up: 'What does the shoot system do?' [It holds up the leaves so they can make food, and it carries water up the stem.] Add one local example: show or name cogon grass and kangkong. Say: 'Cogon grass has many spreading roots and underground stems that hold soil. Kangkong has shoots that grow above water or soil.' Do not state that cogon roots are the deepest or strongest; just say they are many and spreading.
flow.learners: Choose an answer individually and show it. Listen to the explanation and answer the follow-up question. Copy the summary lines into their notebooks.

flow.teacher: Give the exit ticket on paper: 'What is one important job of a plant's roots?' Learners answer in one or two sentences. Expected answer: roots take in water and minerals from the soil and help hold the plant in place. Collect the papers as learners leave or after 4 minutes. If time allows, ask two learners to read their answers aloud. For learners who finish early, give the extension question: 'Name one part of the shoot system and its job.' Remind learners again to wash hands after handling plant materials.
flow.learners: Write their answer to the exit-ticket question on a small piece of paper or in their notebook and submit it. Early finishers answer the extension question.

expectedObservations: The root is usually the first part to appear from the germinating seed and grows downward.
The shoot grows upward and has small leaves.
The root is often longer or more branched than the shoot in young mung bean seedlings.
Fine root hairs can be seen on the root with a hand lens.
The stem holds the leaves up toward the light.

check.question: What is one important job of a plant's roots?
check.answer: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil and help hold the plant in place.
check.why: Root hairs absorb water and dissolved minerals, and the root system anchors the plant so it does not fall over.

days.support: For learners who struggle, give a pre-labeled drawing with three blanks (root, stem, leaf) and let them trace the seedling rather than draw it freehand. Pair them with a stronger learner and ask them to point first, then say the job. Use the sentence frame: 'The ___ helps the plant by ___.' If hand lenses are limited, let pairs share and take turns. Allow answers in the learner's home language first, then help them say it in English.
days.extension: Ask early finishers to compare their seedling with the dry-seed cup and write one difference. Or ask them to draw and label a local plant they know, marking its root system and shoot system, and write one job for each. They may also list two shoot parts (for example, stem and leaves) and state each part's job.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, add a whole-class comparison of the mung bean seedling with the pictures of cogon grass and kangkong: learners identify which parts are root system and which are shoot system and describe one difference. Add a short group presentation where two groups show their labeled diagram and say one job for each system. Use the extra time also for learners to finish and post their drawings, and extend the exit ticket to two sentences: one job of the root system and one job of the shoot system.

days.title: Body and Plant Systems Review and Poster
days.objective: Learners will be able to show understanding of the five human body systems and plant root/shoot systems by completing assessment items and planning a labeled poster.
materials: Learners' labeled diagrams from Days 1–4 (one set per group of 4–6)
Manila paper, one sheet per group of 4–6
Crayons, markers, or colored pencils (enough to share per group)
Masking tape or thumbtacks for posting diagrams (teacher use)
Weekly assessment papers, one per learner
Pencils and erasers, one per learner
Chalkboard or whiteboard with chalk or markers
Optional: pre-germinated mung bean cups from Day 4 for reference

flow.teacher: Greet the class and say: 'This week we learned about body systems and plant systems. Let's see what you remember.' Ask: 'Which body system helps you lift your bag?' [muscular and skeletal systems working together] 'Which plant part takes in water from the soil?' [roots] 'Which plant part makes food using sunlight?' [leaves]. Accept answers from several learners. Then say: 'Today we will review, take a short assessment, and start our poster.'
flow.learners: Learners raise hands and answer the review questions aloud. They listen to the day's plan.

flow.teacher: State the goal: 'Today you will show what you know about the five human body systems and about plant roots and shoots. You will also plan a poster that explains these systems with labels and local examples.' Emphasize that the poster is a team effort and that neat labels help others understand.
flow.learners: Learners listen and ask clarifying questions about the poster task.

flow.teacher: Gallery walk: Have each group tape their labeled diagrams from the week on the wall. Give groups 6 minutes to walk quietly and look at two other groups' diagrams. Ask them to notice one good label and one part they would add. After the walk, call on two or three learners to share. Keep the class in small groups to avoid crowding; if space is tight, pass diagrams group to group instead of walking.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners post their diagrams, walk to view two other groups' work, and discuss one good label and one part they would add.

flow.teacher: Administer the weekly assessment. Remind learners to work quietly and on their own. Read each item aloud once for learners who need support. Collect papers when done. If some learners finish early, ask them to silently plan their poster section on scratch paper.
flow.learners: Learners complete the weekly assessment individually and quietly. Early finishers begin planning their poster section on scratch paper.

flow.teacher: Poster planning: Give each group one manila paper. Explain the sections: (1) five human body systems with labels, (2) plant root and shoot systems with labels, (3) one local plant example (e.g. kangkong or mung bean) with its root and shoot systems labeled and one sentence on why each system matters. Model how to draw the plant with its two systems. Remind them to use local examples from the week. Circulate and ask: 'Which system does this part belong to?' [e.g., roots belong to the root system] 'What job does it do?' [absorb water and minerals]. Supervise any cutting; learners should not cut toward their hands.
flow.learners: In groups of 4–6, learners plan and begin drawing the three poster sections on manila paper, labeling parts and filling in the classification table with one local example.

flow.teacher: Ask: 'How do body systems work together?' [They team up; muscles pull bones, the heart and lungs deliver oxygen, digestion gives nutrients.] 'How do root and shoot systems help a plant?' [Roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant; shoots hold leaves up to sunlight and transport water and food.] Summarize: 'Systems, whether in people or plants, have parts with special jobs that keep the living thing alive.'
flow.learners: Learners answer the questions aloud and help build the summary.

flow.teacher: Exit ticket: Give each learner a small slip of paper. Say: 'Write your answer to this question: Why do the skeletal and muscular systems need each other?' Collect the slips as learners leave. Do not show the answer on the board.
flow.learners: Each learner writes a short answer on a slip of paper and submits it.

expectedObservations: Learners can name the five human body systems and match each to its main job.
Learners can point to and label the root system and shoot system on a plant diagram.
Learners explain that muscles pull on bones to move the body and that bones protect soft organs.
Learners give one local Philippine plant or animal example and its habitat in the classification table.
Groups cooperate to plan poster sections with clear labels.

check.question: Why do the skeletal and muscular systems need each other?
check.answer: Muscles pull on bones to move the body; without bones, muscles would have no rigid levers, and without muscles, bones would not move.
check.why: Bones provide the levers and joints, and muscles provide the pulling force. The two systems work as a team.

days.support: For learners who struggle, provide a labeled diagram with missing words to fill in, pair them with a stronger partner during poster planning, and allow them to answer the exit ticket using a word bank: bones, muscles, pull, move, protect. Read assessment items aloud and give extra time if needed.
days.extension: Early finishers can add a fourth poster section: 'How systems work together' with one sentence and a simple arrow diagram linking two systems, or write three quiz questions about body or plant systems for a classmate to answer.
days.longerPeriod: If the period runs 50–60 minutes, extend the gallery walk to 10 minutes with a feedback slip per diagram, allow 15 minutes for poster planning and drawing, and add a 3-minute group sharing where one member explains their poster plan.

assessment.prompt: When you bend your elbow, what happens to your arm muscles?
choices: The muscle in front shortens and pulls; the muscle in back gets longer.
The muscle in back pushes the bone to bend the arm.
Both muscles push at the same time.
The bone pushes the muscle to bend.
assessment.answer: The muscle in front shortens and pulls; the muscle in back gets longer.
assessment.explanation: Muscles can only pull, not push. To bend the elbow, the biceps (front muscle) contracts and shortens, pulling the forearm bone up. The triceps (back muscle) relaxes and gets longer. Choices B, C, and D are wrong because muscles cannot push and bones do not push muscles.

assessment.prompt: Where does most of the food's nutrients enter the blood?
assessment.explanation: The small intestine has many folds and tiny finger-like villi that absorb nutrients into the blood. The mouth starts digestion, the stomach churns and begins protein breakdown, and the large intestine absorbs water and forms waste.

assessment.prompt: Which path does air take when you breathe in?
assessment.explanation: Air enters through the nose, travels down the trachea (windpipe), reaches the lungs, and oxygen moves into the blood. Choices with stomach are wrong; reversed order is wrong; D is wrong because the order is jumbled — air reaches the trachea only after passing the nose, not before it.

assessment.prompt: A farmer plants mung beans. The first root grows downward. What is one important job of this root?
choices: Take in water and minerals from the soil
assessment.answer: Take in water and minerals from the soil
assessment.explanation: Roots have root hairs that absorb water and dissolved minerals. Leaves make sugar, flowers become fruits or attract pollinators, not roots.

assessment.prompt: After you eat rice, which body system carries the digested nutrients to your muscles?
assessment.explanation: The circulatory system transports digested nutrients in the blood from the small intestine to all body cells. The skeletal system supports and protects, the respiratory system exchanges gases, and the muscular system moves the body.

assessment.prompt: Kangkong stems and leaves are above ground. Which job do the leaves do?
choices: Anchor the plant in the soil
Store water for the plant to drink
assessment.explanation: Kangkong leaves contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis, making sugar using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Roots absorb water and anchor; stems may store some water but leaves' main job is food-making.

assessment.prompt: Name one human body system and describe one way it works with another system to keep you alive.
assessment.answer: Example: The circulatory system carries oxygen picked up by the respiratory system to the muscles. Another example: The muscular system pulls on bones of the skeletal system to move the body.
assessment.explanation: The key is that the learner identifies a system and gives a correct connection: circulatory transports what respiratory brings in; muscular uses skeletal levers; digestive supplies nutrients that circulatory transports. Accept any correct pair with a clear connection.

assessment.prompt: Create a labeled poster. Include these parts: (1) the five human body systems—muscular, skeletal, digestive, circulatory, respiratory—with one label and one job for each; (2) a plant with root system and shoot system labeled; (3) one local plant (e.g. kangkong or mung bean) with root system and shoot system labelled and one sentence on why each system matters to the plant.
assessment.answer: A poster that shows all required labeled diagrams and the habitat table. Example: kangkong as an aquatic/terrestrial plant, shoot system labeled as stems and leaves, root system labeled as roots; human systems each shown with simple drawings and one job.
assessment.explanation: Full marks: all five systems named, drawn and given one correct job (muscular–pulls bones to move; skeletal–shape, support, protection; digestive–breaks food and absorbs nutrients; circulatory–transports oxygen, nutrients, wastes; respiratory–takes in oxygen, removes carbon dioxide); plant drawn with root system and shoot system correctly labelled with one job each. Deduct one point per missing or mislabelled system.

slides.title: Body Systems and Plant Root and Shoot Systems
lines: Grade 4 Science · Term 1 · Week 8
Five 45-minute lessons
slides.notes: How to use this deck: each lesson starts with a "Day" slide. Speaker notes under every slide tell you what to say, what to ask and the answers to expect; they show only in Presenter View, never on the TV. Question slides come before their answer slides, so learners can think before the answer appears. The teacher guide (separate PDF) explains the science behind the week, common wrong ideas, and the full answer key.

slides.title: Day 1: Muscles and Bones
lines: Today: How muscles and bones work together to help us move.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and read the title aloud. Point to your own arm and say: 'Today we will find out what is inside your arm that helps you bend it.' Keep this short — about 1 minute. Ask learners to sit where they can see the TV or board. Tell them they will do a partner activity later, so they should listen carefully now. No answer is needed on this slide; it only sets the goal for the day.

slides.title: What moves when you bend your arm?
lines: Bend your arm slowly.
What do you feel on your upper arm?
slides.notes: Ask learners to bend their arm and feel the top of their upper arm. Give 30 seconds. Call on 2–3 learners: 'What did you feel?' Accept answers like 'something got hard' or 'a muscle.' Do not confirm the word biceps yet — you will name it later. If a learner says 'the bone moves,' praise the observation and say: 'Yes, the bone moves. But what makes it move? We will find out.' This slide activates what learners already know from Grade 3 about the body. Keep it moving — about 2 minutes.

slides.title: Our goal for today
lines: We will learn how muscles pull on bones at joints.
We will learn how bones protect soft organs.
Key words: bones, muscles, joints.
slides.notes: Read the goal aloud in simple words. Say: 'By the end of our lesson, you will be able to explain how your arm bends and why your bones are important.' Point to the three key words and ask the class to repeat them after you: bones, muscles, joints. Tell learners they will answer a short question on paper at the end, so they should listen well. This is the lesson purpose — about 2 minutes. Do not explain the words yet; the next slides will do that.

slides.title: The Skeletal System: Shape and Support
lines: All the bones in your body make up your skeleton.
The skeleton is the skeletal system.
It gives your body shape and holds you up.
Bones are living tissue. They grow and can heal.

image.alt: A front view of a simple human skeleton showing the rib cage and main bones.

slides.notes: Point to the skeleton drawing and say: 'This is your skeleton — all the bones in your body.' Ask: 'What would happen if we had no bones?' [We would be floppy; we could not stand.] Correct the common wrong idea that bones are dry, white, and dead: 'Bones are living. They have blood vessels and nerves, they grow as you grow, and they can heal after a break.' Do not go into bone names beyond skull and ribs today. Spend about 3 minutes here. Ask one learner to gently feel their own forearm bone.

slides.title: Bones protect soft organs
lines: Your skull protects your brain.
Your ribs protect your heart and lungs.
Soft organs need hard bones around them.
slides.notes: Ask learners to gently touch their skull and their ribs. Say: 'Feel how hard your skull is. It protects your brain. Feel your ribs. They make a cage around your heart and lungs.' Ask: 'Why do you think the brain needs a hard cover?' [It is soft and easily hurt.] Avoid saying the heart never gets tired or any other claim you are not sure of. Keep to protection. About 3 minutes. If a learner says bones are just for moving, add: 'Bones also protect and support — they do three jobs.'

slides.title: The Muscular System: Muscles Pull
lines: The muscular system is all your muscles.
A muscle can shorten and pull on a bone.
A muscle cannot push a bone.
Muscles work in pairs to move bones.

image.alt: An upper arm shown bent and straight, with one muscle shortening while its partner relaxes to move the bone.

slides.notes: Hold up the cardboard strip and rubber band. Say: 'The strip is the bone. The rubber band is the muscle. When I pull the rubber band, the strip bends.' Pull it. Then ask: 'Can the rubber band push the strip back?' [No.] Say: 'Muscles only pull. They never push.' This corrects the common misconception that muscles push bones. Ask learners to say the sentence after you: 'Muscles pull, they do not push.' About 5 minutes including the demonstration. Keep the rubber band stretched gently so it does not snap.

slides.title: Muscles work in pairs
lines: The biceps pulls to bend your arm.
The triceps pulls to straighten it.
One muscle relaxes while the other pulls.

image.alt: An upper arm shown bent and straight, with one muscle shortening while its partner relaxes to move the bone.

slides.notes: Point to the drawing and name the muscles: 'The muscle on top of your upper arm is the biceps. The one at the back is the triceps.' Ask learners to feel both while bending and straightening the arm. Ask: 'Which muscle pulls when you bend your arm?' [The biceps.] 'Which one pulls when you straighten it?' [The triceps.] Explain that they take turns — one pulls while the other relaxes. About 5 minutes. If a learner says both muscles pull at the same time, correct gently: 'They take turns so the arm can go both ways.'

slides.title: Feel and draw the arm
lines: 1. In pairs, one partner slowly bends and straightens the arm.
2. The other gently presses the upper arm to feel the muscles.
3. Draw the arm on paper.
4. Label the bones, biceps, triceps, and elbow joint.
Record: which muscle feels hard when the arm bends.

image.alt: An elbow hinge joint shown with the upper and lower arm bones meeting and bending like a door hinge.

slides.notes: Read the steps aloud. Say: 'Press gently. Never twist your partner's arm.' Give 8 minutes. Walk around and ask: 'Which muscle is hard when the arm bends?' [The biceps.] 'Which one is hard when it straightens?' [The triceps.] 'What do we call the place where two bones meet?' [A joint.] Remind learners the elbow is a hinge joint — it bends like a door. In a large class, one partner draws while the other labels, then they swap. Safety: gentle pressing only, no pulling or twisting. About 12 minutes including drawing.

slides.title: Copy this summary
lines: The skeletal system gives my body shape and support.
Bones protect soft organs like my brain, heart, and lungs.
Muscles only pull, never push. They work in pairs.
A joint is where two bones meet and allow movement.
slides.notes: Read each sentence aloud and ask learners to repeat it after you. Ask fill-in-the-blank questions: 'Bones give my body ___ and ___.' [Shape; support.] 'Muscles can only ___, not push.' [Pull.] 'A ___ is where two bones meet.' [Joint.] Give 2 minutes to copy the summary into notebooks. Tell learners: 'You will use these sentences to answer a question on paper.' Check that everyone has started copying before moving on.

slides.title: Which is true about muscles and bones?
lines: Choose the correct statement.
choices: Muscles push bones to move them.
Muscles pull on bones; they cannot push.
Bones are dead and cannot heal.
slides.notes: Read the question and each option aloud. Give 1 minute for learners to write their answer on paper. Do not reveal the answer yet. Walk around to see which option most learners chose. If many choose the first option, that is the common misconception that muscles push — note it for the reveal. Keep the pace quick. About 2 minutes. Remind learners not to call out the answer.

slides.title: The correct answer
lines: Answer: Muscles pull on bones; they cannot push.
Muscles can only shorten and pull.
Pairs of muscles pull in opposite directions to move a bone.
slides.notes: Say: 'The correct answer is the second one — muscles pull on bones; they cannot push.' Explain: 'A muscle can only shorten and pull. To move a bone back and forth, a pair of muscles pulls in opposite directions.' Point back to the muscle pairs drawing. If learners chose option 1, say: 'Remember the rubber band — it could pull but not push.' After this, give the exit ticket on paper: 'Which statement is correct about muscles and bones?' with four options. Collect the slips so you can see who still has the misconception. About 2 minutes.

slides.title: Day 2: Food's Journey
lines: Today: We follow one bite of food through the body.
We learn what happens at each stop.
slides.notes: Greet the class and read the title. Tell learners that today they will follow one bite of food from the mouth to the end of the journey. Keep this to under a minute. Ask: 'What happens to your food after you swallow it?' Take 3–4 answers and write 2–3 on the board without correcting them yet — you will return to these at the end. Common wrong answer: 'The stomach does everything.' Say: 'Let us find out if that is true.'

slides.title: New Words for Today
lines: Digestion — the breaking of food into smaller nutrients the body can use.
Esophagus — the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach.
Nutrient — a part of food the body uses for energy and growth.
slides.notes: Read each word aloud and have the class repeat 'digestion' and 'esophagus' twice, because esophagus is hard to say. Explain in plain language: digestion is like breaking a big piece of food into tiny pieces the body can use. The esophagus is the tube in your throat and chest that leads to the stomach — it is not the windpipe. If a learner says food 'falls' down, say: 'We will see that the esophagus squeezes it down.' Keep this to 2 minutes; the words come back during the lesson.

slides.title: The Digestive System: Our Goal
lines: The digestive system breaks down food.
We can trace the path of food.
We can say what happens at each stop.
At the end, we draw the path in pairs.
slides.notes: Read the goal together with the class. Do not give the order of the organs yet — learners will build the order themselves during the activity. The image on this slide is an unlabeled body outline. Tell them that at the end they will answer one question on paper by themselves. This helps them listen carefully during the lesson. Keep to 1–2 minutes.

slides.title: Digestion Starts in the Mouth
lines: Teeth grind food into smaller pieces.
Saliva makes food wet and starts breaking it down.
Digestion begins here, not in the stomach.
slides.notes: Ask: 'Why do we chew our food?' Expect: 'So it is easier to swallow', 'To make it small.' Add that saliva makes food wet and starts breaking it down, so digestion begins in the mouth. Point to the drawing. Common wrong answer: 'The stomach is where all digestion happens.' Reply: 'The stomach does a big job, but the mouth starts the work.' Say that chewing well helps the next stops do their job. About 2 minutes.

slides.title: The Esophagus Squeezes Food Down
lines: The esophagus is a tube from the mouth to the stomach.
Its muscles squeeze in waves to push food down.
Food is pushed down, not just dropped.
slides.notes: Ask: 'When you swallow, does food just fall down?' Most learners think it falls. Explain that the walls of the esophagus squeeze in waves — like squeezing a toothpaste tube from the bottom up — and this pushes food to the stomach. Use your hand to show a squeezing wave. Stress that the esophagus leads to the stomach, not to the lungs. About 2 minutes.

slides.title: The Stomach Churns Food
lines: The stomach is a bag of muscle.
Its walls squeeze and mix food with juices.
Food becomes a soft, soupy mixture.
Do not open the bag during the demonstration.

image.alt: A cutaway stomach with muscular walls squeezing and mixing food with juices into a soupy mixture.

slides.notes: Do the zip-top bag demonstration beside this slide. Put a bread slice and a little water in the bag, seal it well, and squeeze gently. Ask: 'What is happening to the bread?' Expect: 'It gets soft and mushy.' Say: 'The stomach is a strong bag of muscle; it squeezes food with juices.' Safety: seal the bag fully, squeeze gently so it does not burst, do not let learners open it, do not taste it, and wash hands after. If a learner asks about the juices, say the stomach has juices that help break down food. About 3 minutes.

slides.title: The Small and Large Intestine
lines: The small intestine takes in most nutrients into the blood.
The large intestine takes in water and forms waste.
The body uses the nutrients for energy and growth.
slides.notes: Say it clearly: the small intestine is long and folded, and most nutrients pass into the blood there. The large intestine takes in water and forms waste, which leaves the body. Common wrong answer: 'The stomach absorbs all the food.' Reply: 'Digestion starts in the mouth; the stomach churns and mixes food with juices; the small intestine finishes the job and takes in most nutrients.' Do not use the word 'poop' in teacher talk unless learners use it first; say 'waste'. Keep to 2 minutes.

slides.title: Draw the Food Path
lines: 1. In pairs, take one big paper.
2. Draw a body outline.
3. Draw arrows: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine.
4. Label each part and write one job.
5. Record: check that all 5 stops are labeled.
slides.notes: Give clear instructions before handing out materials. One pair per table collects materials to save time. Walk around and ask pairs: 'Which organ takes in most nutrients?' and 'Which one takes in water?' Give a 2-minute warning. In a large class, circulate in a fixed order (row by row) so every pair gets checked. If a pair draws the stomach as the biggest stop, respond: 'Digestion starts in the mouth; the stomach churns and mixes food with juices; the small intestine finishes the job and takes in most nutrients.' Pairs exchange papers at the end to check labels. About 12 minutes.

slides.title: Where does most nutrient absorption happen?
slides.notes: Read the question and all four choices aloud. Give 30 seconds of quiet thinking time, then have learners vote by raising hands. Count and do not say the answer yet. If many choose the stomach, say: 'The stomach churns and starts breaking down proteins, but most nutrients are taken in later in the tube.' Do not comment on individual answers. This is a quick check for the whole class before the reveal.

slides.title: Most Nutrients Go In Here
lines: The right answer is the small intestine.
It is long and folded, so nutrients pass into the blood there.
The stomach mostly churns food with juices.
slides.notes: Confirm the answer and give the reason in plain words: the small intestine is long and folded, so it can take in many nutrients into the blood; the stomach mostly churns and starts breaking down proteins. Ask learners to fix their pair drawings if they labeled the stomach as the main absorber. Return to the board answers from the start of the lesson and ask which ones to keep and which to change. Keep to 2 minutes.

slides.title: Day 3: Circulation and Breathing
lines: Today: How the heart and lungs work together.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and read the title together. Remind learners that last time they learned how food is digested; today they find out how oxygen gets to every cell and how waste gas leaves the body. Ask: 'What do you already know about the heart and lungs?' Accept all answers. Tell them they will do a short, safe pulse check later, so they need to keep the floor clear.

slides.title: What changes when you run fast?
lines: Talk with your partner: what changes in your body when you run fast?
slides.notes: Give 30 seconds for partner talk, then take 2–3 answers. Expect: faster breathing, faster heartbeat, sweating, tired legs. Write 'breathe faster' and 'heart beats faster' on the board. Do not correct guesses yet; these will be explained during the lesson. In large classes, use a quick 'hands up' count to keep responses short.

slides.title: The Circulatory and Respiratory Systems: Our Goal
lines: The circulatory system moves blood.
Describe how the heart pumps blood.
Describe how the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
slides.notes: Read the goal aloud. Say: 'By the end, you should be able to explain why your breathing speeds up after jumping.' Ask one learner to repeat the goal in their own words. Check that learners understand the words 'exchange' (swap) and 'oxygen' (a gas in air we need). Keep this short, about 1 minute, so the main activities have time.

slides.title: The Circulatory System: Heart Pump
lines: The circulatory system includes the heart and blood vessels.
The heart is a muscle about the size of your fist.
It pumps blood through tubes called blood vessels.
It works all the time.
slides.notes: Point to your own chest. Say: 'The heart is a muscle that pumps blood around your body all the time.' Ask: 'Where can you feel your heart beating?' Expect: wrist, neck, chest. Clarify that blood travels in blood vessels, which are tubes. Avoid saying the heart 'never gets tired'; instead say it works all the time and rests between beats. This slide takes about 3 minutes.

slides.title: Words to know
lines: Pulse — the beat you feel when the heart pumps blood.
Blood vessels — tubes that carry blood around the body.
slides.notes: Read each term and meaning, then have the class repeat the words. Demonstrate finding a pulse on your wrist using two fingers, not the thumb. Say: 'Two fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has its own pulse. Use only the wrist, never the neck. Press lightly.' Learners copy both terms into their notebooks. About 3 minutes. This prepares them for the pulse activity.

slides.title: Blood carries oxygen and food
lines: Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It carries carbon dioxide away from cells.
slides.notes: Say: 'Blood is like a delivery truck. It brings oxygen and nutrients to cells and takes away carbon dioxide.' Explain that carbon dioxide is a waste gas made by cells. Ask: 'What do you think happens if cells do not get oxygen?' Expect: they cannot work well. Do not overcomplicate; keep answers simple. About 2 minutes.

slides.title: Count your pulse
lines: 1. Sit down and find your pulse.
2. Count beats for 15 seconds.
3. Do 10 gentle jumps.
4. Count again and compare.
Record: pulse before and after.
slides.notes: Model the pulse check. Safety: clear floor space before jumping; learners with difficulty breathing or asthma may count breaths instead. Time 15 seconds for each count. After jumping, ask: 'What happened to your pulse?' Expect it went up. Ask: 'Why?' Expect muscles need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. Write a few before and after numbers on the board. About 6 minutes.

slides.title: The Respiratory System: Lungs
lines: The respiratory system includes the lungs.
Lungs bring oxygen into the blood.
They remove carbon dioxide from the blood.

image.alt: Oxygen moves from the air in the lungs into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves out.

slides.notes: Point to the illustration. Say: 'Air goes in through your nose or mouth, down the windpipe (trachea), and into your lungs. Oxygen from the air moves into your blood. Carbon dioxide leaves your blood and goes out when you breathe out.' Ask: 'What gas do we breathe in?' (oxygen) 'What gas do we breathe out?' (carbon dioxide). Be careful not to say breathing is respiration; explain that breathing brings oxygen to the blood. About 3 minutes.

slides.title: Heart and lungs work as a team
lines: The circulatory system and respiratory system work together.
Lungs add oxygen to the blood.
The heart pumps the blood to the body.
Blood brings carbon dioxide back to the lungs.
slides.notes: Draw the loop on the board: lungs → heart → body → heart → lungs. Use red for oxygen-rich blood and blue for carbon dioxide-rich blood. Say: 'Blood is always red — brighter red when it carries more oxygen, darker red when it carries less. Blue is only a drawing colour we use to show blood heading back to the lungs.' Have learners copy the loop into notebooks and label 'oxygen in' and 'carbon dioxide out'. Ask: 'Why must the heart and lungs work together?' Expect: the lungs add oxygen; the heart pumps the blood that carries it. About 4 minutes.

slides.title: What does blood carry to cells?
slides.notes: Read the question and choices aloud. Give 1 minute of thinking time, then ask learners to show their answer by raising 1, 2, 3, or 4 fingers. Do not reveal the answer yet. Common wrong answer: 'only water' — respond by reminding them that blood carries oxygen and nutrients to cells. About 2 minutes.

slides.title: Answer: Oxygen and nutrients
lines: Correct: Oxygen and nutrients.
Blood delivers oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries carbon dioxide away.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct answer. Explain: 'Blood is the delivery truck. It brings oxygen and nutrients to cells and carries carbon dioxide away.' Ask learners who chose a wrong answer to explain what they now know. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'Why does your breathing speed up after jumping?' Collect papers. Look for answers mentioning oxygen and carbon dioxide. About 4 minutes.

slides.title: Day 4: Roots Below, Shoots Above
lines: Today: We observe a sprouting seed and learn what roots and shoots do.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and connect to the week's body systems lessons in one sentence: we studied how the human body works, and now we study how a plant's parts work. Read the 'Today' line aloud. Tell learners that today they will use real sprouting mung bean seeds. Set the tone that this is careful observation, not play. Timing: about 1 minute. Ask: 'What plant parts do you already know?' Accept answers such as roots, stem, leaves, flower. Do not correct yet; the next slides build the correct ideas. Remind learners that they will wash hands after handling the cups and cotton.

slides.title: Where do roots grow?
lines: Where do you think a plant's roots grow?
Why do you think they grow there?
slides.notes: This activates what learners already notice about plants. Ask the first question and take 2–3 answers. Most learners will say roots grow under the ground. Then ask why. Expect answers like 'to get water' or 'to hold the plant.' Do not confirm or correct yet; say, 'We will find out today by looking closely.' If a learner says 'roots eat soil,' note it silently and address it during the lesson with the idea that roots take in water and minerals while leaves make food. Timing: 2–3 minutes. Keep the pace quick so all learners answer to a partner first.

slides.title: Two plant system words
lines: Root — the plant part usually below ground that takes in water and minerals.
Stem — the part that holds up leaves and carries water and food.
Shoot system — all the above-ground parts: stem, leaves, buds, flowers, fruits.
slides.notes: Read each term aloud and have learners repeat 'root' and 'shoot system' after you. Explain that the root system includes all the roots, and the shoot system includes everything above ground. Point out that a seed is not part of the shoot system; it is the young plant's stored food and starting point. Give one local example orally: kangkong shoots are the parts we see above the ground or water. Ask learners to copy the three meanings into their notebooks. Timing: 3 minutes. Check that learners write 'above-ground' correctly by spelling it aloud once.

slides.title: Which part comes out first?
lines: A sprouting seed usually sends its root down first.
Then the shoot grows up toward the light.

image.alt: A germinating seed underground, with its root growing downward and a small shoot beginning to grow upward, shown in cutaway.

slides.notes: Use the drawing to show the root going down and the shoot going up. Say: 'In many seeds, the root appears first.' Be careful not to say this is always true for every plant; say 'usually' or 'in many seeds.' Ask: 'Why is it useful for the root to go down first?' [It can reach water and hold the plant in place.] For Grade 4, keep the answer simple: water and anchoring. Timing: 2–3 minutes. Link to the seedling cups they will observe: they should check which part is longer and which way each part grows.

slides.title: What do roots do?
lines: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil.
Roots also hold the plant in place so it does not fall over.

image.alt: A plant with its roots reaching down into a cutaway patch of soil, the fine root tips spreading among the soil grains.

slides.notes: Say the two main jobs clearly: taking in water and minerals, and anchoring the plant. Correct the common misconception that plants get their food from the soil: 'Roots take in water and minerals, but the plant makes its own food in its leaves using sunlight.' Do not say roots absorb sugar from the soil. Ask learners to point to the drawing and say where the water enters the plant. Timing: 3 minutes. If learners say roots 'eat' soil, respond: 'Roots take in water and minerals; the leaves make the food.'

slides.title: Observe your sprouting seed
lines: 1. Look closely at your cup. Find the root and the shoot.
2. Use a hand lens to see the fine root hairs.
3. Draw and label: root, shoot, leaves.
4. Write one job for the root system and one for the shoot system.
slides.notes: Give clear steps. Hand one cup per pair and one hand lens per pair; if lenses are few, let pairs take turns. Remind learners: wash hands after handling the cups and cotton, do not eat the seeds, and do not pull the seedlings out. Let pairs observe for 3 minutes, then draw and label. Ask: 'Which is longer, the root or the shoot?' and 'Which way does each grow?' Expected: the root is usually longer and grows down; the shoot grows up. Circulate to check labels. In large classes, have one materials monitor per group return the cups. Timing: 12–15 minutes.

slides.title: What is the main job of roots?
choices: To take in water and minerals from the soil
To carry food down to the leaves
slides.notes: Ask learners to answer on their paper or show 1, 2, 3, or 4 with their fingers. Do not say the answer yet. This checks whether they know the root's job after the activity. A common wrong answer is 'to make food using sunlight,' which is the leaf's job. If many choose that, remind them that the leaves make food. Give about 1 minute for thinking and answering before revealing. Do not read the answer aloud or hint by pointing. Keep the choices on the screen only.

slides.title: The answer is about water
lines: Roots take in water and minerals from the soil.
They also hold the plant in place.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct choice and explain in one sentence: roots take in water and minerals and hold the plant. Briefly explain why the other choices are wrong: leaves make food, the stem carries water and food, and flowers are part of the shoot system. Ask: 'What would happen to a plant if its roots were cut off?' [It could not take in water and would wilt, and it would not be held in place.] Keep the answer simple and avoid saying the plant would always die, because some plants can regrow roots. Timing: 2 minutes.

slides.title: What we learned today
lines: The root system is usually below ground. It takes in water and minerals and holds the plant.
The shoot system is above ground. Its stem holds up leaves so they can make food.
The skeletal system and muscular system are two body systems.

image.alt: A black-and-white cross-section illustration of a young plant with a visible root system below ground and a shoot system (stem and leaves) above ground.

slides.notes: Have learners copy these two lines into their notebooks. Read them aloud together once. Point to the drawing and ask learners to name one part of the shoot system they can see [stem, leaves, flower]. Then give the exit ticket on paper: 'What is one important job of a plant's roots?' Expected answer: roots take in water and minerals and hold the plant in place. Collect answers. Remind everyone to wash hands after handling plant materials. Timing: 5–7 minutes including the exit ticket.

slides.title: Day 5: Review and Poster
lines: Today: We review body and plant systems, take a short assessment, and plan a poster.
slides.notes: Welcome the class and read the slide aloud. Remind learners that this is the last day of the week's topic. Say that today they will show what they learned and start a poster. Keep this short; the goal is to set a calm, focused tone before the review questions. Ask: 'What did we study this week?' Expect answers like body systems, bones, muscles, roots, shoots. Praise any correct recall.

slides.title: What Do You Remember?
lines: Which system helps you lift a bag?
Which plant part takes in water?
slides.notes: Use this slide to activate prior knowledge. Ask the questions one at a time and wait 5 seconds before calling on learners. Expected answers: the skeletal and muscular systems work together to lift a bag; roots take in water. If a learner says leaves take in water, respond: 'Leaves make food, but roots absorb water and minerals. Let's check our plant diagram later.' Accept answers from several learners so more voices are heard.

slides.title: Our Goal for Today
lines: Show what you know about body systems.
Show what you know about plant roots and shoots.
Plan a labeled poster with local examples.
slides.notes: State the lesson goal clearly. Explain that the poster is a group task where every member helps. Mention that labels and local examples make a poster easy to understand. Ask: 'What makes a good label?' Expect answers like it points to the right part and is spelled correctly. Tell learners they will first walk around to see other groups' diagrams, then take a short assessment, then plan the poster.

slides.title: Gallery Walk Steps
lines: 1. Post your group's diagrams on the wall.
2. Walk quietly to two other groups' diagrams.
3. Notice one good label and one part to add.
4. Share with your group.
Record: one good label and one part to add.
slides.notes: Give clear instructions before learners move. Set a 6-minute limit. To avoid crowding in large classes, send only two groups at a time or pass diagrams group to group. Walk among learners and listen for science talk. Ask: 'Why is this label helpful?' Expect answers like it points clearly to the part. If learners just say 'nice drawing', redirect: 'What science word did they use?' Collect feedback aloud after the walk.

slides.title: Assessment Time
lines: Work quietly and on your own.
Read each item carefully.
Raise your hand if you need help reading.
slides.notes: Explain that this short assessment shows what learners understood this week. Remind them to keep their eyes on their own paper. Read each item aloud once for the class. If a learner asks for an answer, say: 'Do your best and answer what you know.' Collect papers when most learners are done. Keep the atmosphere calm and encouraging; this is not a punishment.

slides.title: Poster Plan Steps
lines: 1. Get one manila paper per group.
2. Draw and label the five body systems.
3. Draw and label the plant root and shoot systems.
4. Make a table: organism, habitat, system or part.
Record: one local plant or animal example.
slides.notes: Model how to divide the manila paper into three sections. Show a simple table on the board with three columns. Remind learners to use local examples from the week, such as cogon grass or kangkong. Circulate and ask: 'Which system does this part belong to?' and 'What job does it do?' If a group cannot think of a local example, suggest a plant they saw this week. Supervise any cutting; learners should cut away from their hands and share scissors safely.

slides.title: Labeled Diagrams Help Us Explain
lines: A label points to a part and names it.
Clear labels help others understand your poster.
Use local examples to make it real.

image.alt: A single flowering plant stem with leaves and one flower attached along its length.

slides.notes: Point to the drawing and ask learners to name the parts they see: stem, leaves, flower. Ask: 'Which system is this?' [shoot system] 'What job does the stem do?' [holds up leaves and moves water and food] Explain that a clear label has a line pointing exactly to the part and a word naming it. Tell learners their poster should use the same clear style. Keep this brief so poster work continues.

slides.title: Systems Work Together
lines: Body systems team up to keep us alive.
Roots take in water and minerals and hold the plant.
Shoots hold leaves up to sunlight and move water and food.
slides.notes: Read the summary aloud and have learners repeat the key ideas. Ask: 'How do muscles and bones work as a team?' [muscles pull, bones are levers] 'How do roots and shoots help each other?' [roots supply water and minerals; shoots make food and support the plant] Correct the idea that plants eat soil: plants make their own food in the leaves. Tell learners to copy the summary into their notebooks if time allows.

slides.title: Which two systems help you move?
lines: Which two systems work together to move your arm?
slides.notes: Use this as a quick oral check before the exit ticket, or skip it if time is short. Do not reveal the answer on the slide; ask learners to vote by raising fingers. Expected answer: skeletal and muscular. If many choose digestive and circulatory, say: 'Digestion gives energy and blood carries it, but which parts actually pull and move the arm?' Then show the next slide to reveal the correct answer and give the reason.

slides.title: Answer: Skeletal and Muscular
lines: Muscles pull on bones to move the body.
Bones act as levers, and joints let them bend.
slides.notes: Reveal the correct answer and explain: muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs. Bones give the body a frame and act as levers at joints. Ask: 'What would happen if we had no bones?' [muscles would have nothing to pull] 'What if we had no muscles?' [bones would not move] Connect to the exit ticket by reminding learners to explain the teamwork of the two systems. Keep this to one minute so learners have time to write.
